title: Tomato Soup
description: A bright, classic tomato soup made with pantry tomatoes, aromatic vegetables, and basil for an easy American comfort-food lunch.
ingredients: 2 cans (28 oz each) whole peeled tomatoes
instructions: Heat the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium heat, add the onion, carrots, and celery, and cook for 8 minutes until the vegetables soften without taking on dark color.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste, then cook for about 1 minute while stirring constantly so the paste darkens slightly and the garlic smells fragrant but does not burn.
Add the whole tomatoes with their juices, crushing each tomato carefully against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon to create evenly sized pieces before simmering.
Pour in the vegetable broth, oregano, salt, and pepper, scrape the bottom of the pot to release any flavorful browned bits, and bring the mixture to a gentle boil.
Lower the heat, partially cover the pot, and simmer for 25 minutes until the carrots are completely tender and the tomato flavor tastes rounded rather than raw or sharply acidic.
Remove the pot from the heat, add the basil, and blend with an immersion blender until the soup is smooth, keeping the blade fully submerged to prevent hot splashes.
Return the soup to low heat, taste carefully, and add the optional sugar only if the tomatoes remain unusually acidic; adjust salt and pepper in small amounts.
Ladle the hot soup into warmed bowls and serve with grilled cheese, crackers, or crusty bread while the soup is smooth, fragrant, and steaming.
tips: Use good-quality whole canned tomatoes for consistent flavor.
Blend in batches with a countertop blender only after cooling slightly.
Add sugar only after tasting the finished soup.
commonMistakes: Browning the garlic makes the soup bitter.
A vigorous boil can reduce the soup too quickly.
Overfilling a blender with hot soup is unsafe.
substitutions: Use chicken broth instead of vegetable broth.
Replace fresh basil with 1 teaspoon dried basil.
Use fire-roasted tomatoes for a smokier flavor.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup in a covered container for up to 4 days.
Reheat gently on the stovetop until steaming.
Freeze portions for up to 3 months and thaw overnight in the refrigerator.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Creamy Tomato Soup
description: Silky creamy tomato soup with garlic, basil, Parmesan, and a gentle splash of cream for a rich, cozy bowl.
instructions: Warm the olive oil in a Dutch oven over medium heat, add the onion, and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until soft and translucent without allowing the edges to scorch.
Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds, then sprinkle in the flour and cook for 1 minute so the raw flour taste disappears while the mixture stays pale.
Slowly whisk in the vegetable broth until no flour lumps remain, then add the crushed tomatoes, sugar, salt, and pepper and stir until evenly combined.
Bring the soup just to a simmer, reduce the heat to medium-low, and cook uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent tomato solids from catching on the bottom.
Add the fresh basil, remove the pot from direct heat, and blend until completely smooth with an immersion blender held below the surface to avoid splashing hot liquid.
Return the pot to low heat and stir in the heavy cream gradually, keeping the soup below a boil so the dairy remains smooth instead of separating.
Add the Parmesan a small handful at a time, stirring until each addition melts, then taste and adjust the salt, pepper, or sugar only as needed.
Serve immediately in warm bowls with extra basil or Parmesan, and pair with toasted bread or grilled cheese for a complete comfort-food meal.
tips: Take the pot off direct heat before blending.
Keep the soup below a boil after adding cream.
Finely grated Parmesan melts more smoothly.
commonMistakes: Adding cream during a hard boil can make it separate.
Uncooked flour leaves a pasty taste.
Too much sugar hides the natural tomato flavor.
substitutions: Use half-and-half for a lighter finish.
Use chicken broth if the soup does not need to be vegetarian.
Use pecorino Romano in place of Parmesan.
storage: Refrigerate in a covered container for up to 4 days.
Reheat slowly over medium-low heat without boiling.
Freeze before adding cream for the smoothest thawed texture.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Potato Soup
description: Thick loaded potato soup with tender russets, smoky bacon, cheddar, and a creamy broth that stays hearty rather than gluey.
ingredients: 2 1/2 lb russet potatoes, peeled and cubed
instructions: Place the chopped bacon in a cold Dutch oven, set it over medium heat, and cook slowly until crisp and the fat has rendered, then transfer the bacon to a lined plate.
Leave about 2 tablespoons of bacon fat in the pot, add the onion, and cook for 5 minutes until tender before stirring in the garlic for another 30 seconds.
Sprinkle the flour over the onions and stir continuously for 1 minute, making sure no dry pockets remain and the flour does not darken or stick to the pot.
Add the chicken broth in several small additions while whisking, then stir in the potatoes, salt, and pepper and bring the liquid to a gentle simmer.
Cover partially and cook for 15 to 18 minutes until a fork slides easily into the potatoes, stirring near the bottom occasionally so the thickening soup does not scorch.
Mash about one-third of the potatoes directly in the pot to thicken the broth while leaving plenty of intact cubes for a hearty, clearly textured finished soup.
Reduce the heat to low, stir in the milk and sour cream until smooth, then add the cheddar gradually and stop heating before the soup reaches a boil.
Taste and adjust seasoning, ladle into bowls, and top with the reserved bacon and chives so every serving receives crisp, fresh contrast.
tips: Cut potatoes into equal cubes for even cooking.
Mash only part of the potatoes for the best texture.
Grate cheese from a block for smooth melting.
commonMistakes: Overblending russet potatoes can make the soup gluey.
Boiling dairy may split the soup.
Packaged shredded cheese can melt unevenly.
substitutions: Use vegetable broth and omit bacon for a vegetarian version.
Use Yukon Gold potatoes for a creamier texture.
Replace sour cream with plain Greek yogurt off the heat.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup for up to 4 days.
Reheat gently with a splash of broth or milk.
Freezing is not recommended because potatoes and dairy may separate.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Broccoli Cheddar Soup
description: Creamy broccoli cheddar soup packed with tender florets, carrots, and freshly grated sharp cheese in every spoonful.
instructions: Melt the butter in a heavy pot over medium heat, add the onion, and cook for 5 to 6 minutes until soft and translucent without browning the butter.
Sprinkle the flour evenly over the onions and whisk for 1 to 2 minutes until the mixture bubbles and loses its raw flour aroma while remaining light in color.
Pour in the vegetable broth a little at a time while whisking constantly, then add the milk and half-and-half and continue whisking until completely smooth.
Add the broccoli, grated carrot, garlic powder, salt, and pepper, then bring the soup to a very gentle simmer rather than a rapid boil.
Reduce the heat to medium-low, cover partially, and cook for 15 minutes until the broccoli stems are tender when pierced but the florets still hold their shape.
For a thicker texture, briefly press a few broccoli pieces against the side of the pot with a spoon while keeping most florets whole and recognizable.
Turn the heat to its lowest setting and add the cheddar in small handfuls, stirring until each portion melts before adding the next so the soup stays creamy.
Taste for seasoning and serve promptly, avoiding further boiling, with crusty bread or a sandwich while the cheese sauce remains smooth and glossy.
tips: Freshly grate cheddar because anti-caking powder can make soup grainy.
Keep the florets small enough for comfortable spoonfuls.
Use low heat when melting the cheese.
commonMistakes: Boiling cheese can make it oily and grainy.
Adding all the liquid at once encourages flour lumps.
Large broccoli stems may remain tough.
substitutions: Use chicken broth instead of vegetable broth.
Use mild cheddar for a gentler cheese flavor.
Replace half-and-half with additional whole milk.
storage: Refrigerate covered for up to 3 days.
Reheat slowly while stirring and do not boil.
Freezing is not recommended because the dairy sauce may separate.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Clam Chowder
description: New England-style clam chowder with tender clams, potatoes, bacon, and a creamy savory broth seasoned with thyme.
ingredients: 3 cans (6.5 oz each) chopped clams, drained with liquid reserved
Chopped parsley and oyster crackers, for serving
instructions: Cook the diced bacon in a heavy pot over medium heat until crisp and its fat has rendered, then move the bacon to a plate while keeping 2 tablespoons of fat in the pot.
Add the onion and celery to the rendered fat and cook for 6 minutes until softened, then stir in the garlic and cook only until fragrant.
Sprinkle the flour over the vegetables and stir for 1 minute, coating every piece and scraping the bottom so the thickener cooks without scorching.
Gradually whisk in the bottled clam juice, reserved canned-clam liquid, and chicken broth until smooth, then add the potatoes, thyme, and bay leaf.
Bring the chowder to a gentle simmer, partially cover, and cook for 15 to 18 minutes until the potatoes are fork-tender but have not broken apart.
Lower the heat, stir in the cream, and warm for 3 minutes without boiling so the broth stays smooth and the potatoes retain their shape.
Add the drained clams and most of the bacon, then cook for only 2 to 3 minutes until the clams are heated through because prolonged cooking makes them rubbery.
Remove the bay leaf, taste and adjust salt and pepper, then serve with parsley, the remaining bacon, and oyster crackers for a crisp finish.
tips: Reserve all canned-clam liquid for deeper flavor.
Add clams only near the end of cooking.
Dice potatoes evenly so they become tender together.
commonMistakes: Long cooking makes clams chewy.
Boiling after adding cream can cause separation.
Adding salt before tasting the clam liquid may over-season the chowder.
substitutions: Use russet potatoes for a softer, thicker chowder.
Replace chicken broth with additional clam juice.
Use half-and-half for a lighter broth.
storage: Refrigerate promptly in a covered container for up to 3 days.
Reheat gently to steaming without boiling.
Freezing is not recommended because cream and potatoes lose texture.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Chicken Tortilla Soup
description: A zesty chicken tortilla soup with tomatoes, black beans, corn, smoky spices, and crisp tortilla strips for topping.
ingredients: Avocado, cilantro, and lime wedges, for serving
instructions: Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a soup pot over medium heat, add the onion and jalapeño, and cook for 6 minutes until softened without darkening the vegetables.
Stir in the garlic, cumin, and chili powder and cook for 30 seconds, moving the spices constantly so they bloom in the oil but do not scorch.
Add the tomatoes and chicken broth, scrape up any seasoned bits from the bottom, and bring the mixture to a steady but gentle simmer.
Stir in the black beans and corn, partially cover the pot, and simmer for 15 minutes so the broth develops flavor while the vegetables stay intact.
Add the shredded cooked chicken and simmer for another 5 minutes, just long enough to heat it thoroughly without drying the tender meat.
Meanwhile, heat the remaining oil in a wide skillet and cook the tortilla strips in batches until crisp and golden, then drain and season lightly with salt.
Stir lime juice into the soup, taste carefully, and adjust the salt, cumin, or lime a little at a time until the broth tastes balanced and lively.
Ladle into bowls and add avocado, cilantro, lime, and crisp tortilla strips only at serving time so the toppings retain their contrasting textures.
tips: Use rotisserie chicken for a fast weeknight version.
Add tortilla strips immediately before eating.
Seed the jalapeño for gentler heat.
commonMistakes: Boiling cooked chicken too long makes it dry.
Soft tortilla strips lose their crisp contrast.
Undrained beans can make the broth muddy.
substitutions: Use pinto beans instead of black beans.
Use leftover turkey in place of chicken.
Bake tortilla strips at 400°F instead of frying.
storage: Refrigerate soup without toppings for up to 4 days.
Reheat until steaming and add fresh toppings afterward.
Freeze the soup base for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Taco Soup

imageCredit.text: Photo by Collin Harvey, CC BY 2.0

description: A fast one-pot taco soup loaded with seasoned ground beef, beans, corn, tomatoes, and familiar Tex-Mex toppings.
ingredients: 1 can (10 oz) tomatoes with green chiles
Shredded cheese, sour cream, avocado, and tortilla chips, for serving
instructions: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat, add the ground beef and onion, and cook for 7 to 8 minutes while breaking the meat into small crumbles.
Drain excess grease carefully if necessary, then add the garlic and taco seasoning and stir for 30 seconds until the spices become fragrant.
Pour in both cans of tomatoes and the beef broth, scraping the bottom of the pot with a wooden spoon to release all browned seasoning and meat bits.
Add the black beans, pinto beans, corn, and salt, stir thoroughly, and bring the soup to a gentle boil over medium-high heat.
Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the broth thickens slightly and the flavors blend.
Check that the beef is fully cooked and the beans are hot, then taste the broth before adding more salt because taco seasoning and canned tomatoes vary.
Let the soup rest off the heat for 5 minutes so the broth settles and thickens enough to hold the meat, beans, and corn in each spoonful.
Serve hot and let each person add cheese, sour cream, avocado, and crushed tortilla chips so the toppings stay fresh and crisp.
tips: Rinse canned beans to control sodium and keep the broth clear.
Brown the beef well before adding liquid.
Offer toppings separately for easy customization.
commonMistakes: Leaving excess beef grease makes the soup heavy.
Adding extra salt before tasting can over-season it.
Cooking toppings in the soup removes their fresh texture.
substitutions: Use ground turkey instead of beef.
Use kidney beans in place of pinto beans.
Add chopped jalapeño for more heat.
storage: Refrigerate the cooled soup for up to 4 days.
Store fresh toppings separately.
Freeze the soup without dairy toppings for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: French Onion Soup
description: Deeply caramelized onion soup with savory beef broth, toasted baguette, and a bubbling Gruyère cheese cap.
instructions: Melt the butter with the oil in a wide heavy pot over medium heat, add the sliced onions and salt, and stir until every strand is lightly coated.
Cook the onions over medium-low heat for 40 to 50 minutes, stirring more often as they darken, until they are deeply golden, soft, and reduced in volume.
Sprinkle in the sugar only after the onions have softened, then add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds without allowing either ingredient to burn.
Pour in the wine and scrape the bottom thoroughly, simmering for 3 to 4 minutes until the sharp alcohol aroma fades and the liquid reduces.
Add the beef broth, thyme, bay leaf, Worcestershire sauce, and pepper, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook uncovered for 25 minutes.
While the soup simmers, toast the baguette slices at 400°F until dry and golden on both sides so they can support the cheese without immediately dissolving.
Remove the bay leaf, taste and adjust seasoning, then divide the hot soup among broiler-safe bowls set securely on a rimmed baking sheet.
Float two toast slices on each bowl, cover generously with Gruyère, and broil while watching continuously until the cheese bubbles and develops golden spots.
tips: Low, patient heat produces sweet onions without burning.
Use genuinely broiler-safe bowls.
Toast bread thoroughly before floating it on the soup.
commonMistakes: High heat burns onions before they caramelize.
Crowding very small pots steams the onions.
Walking away from the broiler can scorch the cheese quickly.
substitutions: Use Swiss cheese instead of Gruyère.
Use additional broth in place of wine.
Use vegetable broth for a lighter vegetarian variation.
storage: Refrigerate soup separately from bread and cheese for up to 4 days.
Reheat the soup before assembling fresh cheese toasts.
Freeze the un-topped soup for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Beef Barley Soup
description: Hearty beef barley soup with browned chuck, tender vegetables, and chewy pearl barley in a rich savory broth.
ingredients: 2 lb beef chuck, cut into 1-inch cubes
instructions: Pat the beef cubes completely dry and season with salt and pepper, then heat 1 tablespoon oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat until shimmering.
Brown the beef in two uncrowded batches for 3 to 4 minutes per side, transferring each batch to a plate only after a deep crust has developed.
Reduce the heat to medium, add the remaining oil, onion, carrots, and celery, and cook for 7 minutes while scraping up browned bits from the pot.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste and cook for 1 minute until the paste darkens slightly, taking care that the garlic does not scorch.
Return the beef and its juices to the pot, add the broth, thyme, bay leaves, and Worcestershire sauce, and bring everything to a gentle simmer.
Cover partially and simmer for 45 minutes, then stir in the rinsed pearl barley and continue cooking for 40 to 45 minutes until both beef and barley are tender.
Stir several times near the end because barley settles and thickens the broth, adding a splash of water or broth if the soup becomes thicker than desired.
Discard the bay leaves, taste and adjust salt and pepper, then finish with parsley and serve hot after a brief 5-minute rest.
tips: Dry and brown beef in batches for a flavorful broth.
Rinse barley before adding it.
Add extra broth if leftovers become very thick.
commonMistakes: Crowded beef steams instead of browning.
Adding barley too early can make it overly soft.
Forgetting to stir may let barley stick to the pot.
substitutions: Use stew meat if chuck is unavailable.
Use quick-cooking barley and add it later according to package directions.
Add mushrooms with the vegetables for extra savory flavor.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup for up to 4 days.
Reheat with extra broth because barley absorbs liquid.
Freeze in airtight portions for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura

title: Split Pea Soup
description: Classic split pea soup simmered with smoky ham, tender vegetables, and herbs until naturally thick and comforting.
ingredients: 1 lb dried green split peas, sorted and rinsed
1 meaty ham bone or smoked ham hock
instructions: Spread the split peas on a tray, remove any small stones or damaged peas, and rinse them under cool water until the draining water runs mostly clear.
Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat, add the onion, carrots, and celery, and cook for 7 minutes until softened but not deeply browned.
Stir in the garlic and thyme for 30 seconds, then add the split peas, ham bone, chicken broth, bay leaf, and black pepper.
Bring the pot to a gentle boil, skim away any foam from the surface, then reduce the heat so the soup maintains a quiet, steady simmer.
Partially cover and cook for 60 to 75 minutes, stirring more frequently as the peas soften, until they break down and the soup becomes thick and creamy.
Transfer the ham bone to a plate, remove usable meat when cool enough to handle, and discard the bone, skin, and any large pieces of fat.
Return the picked meat and diced cooked ham to the pot, simmer for another 5 minutes, and add broth or water if the texture is thicker than preferred.
Remove the bay leaf, taste before adding salt because ham can be salty, then serve hot with black pepper and crusty bread.
tips: Split peas do not need soaking, but they must be sorted and rinsed.
Stir often once the soup begins to thicken.
Season with salt only after the ham has flavored the broth.
commonMistakes: High heat can scorch thick pea soup on the bottom.
Salting early may make a ham-based soup too salty.
Old dried peas may require extra simmering time.
substitutions: Use a smoked turkey leg instead of ham.
Use vegetable broth and omit meat for a vegetarian soup.
Add a diced potato for an even heartier texture.
storage: Refrigerate cooled soup for up to 4 days.
Thin with broth or water while reheating.
Freeze in airtight portions for up to 3 months.
author: Thejan Mahakumbura
